title: Act 11: The Man Who Picked Up a Handful of Salt

beats.text: *Mohandas Gandhi* was a trained barrister working in South Africa
when he was thrown out of a first-class railway carriage he had a valid ticket for, because of his skin.
He spent that night on a cold platform, and he spent the next twenty years developing a method.
He came back to India in *1915* and did something the earlier nationalist leaders hadn't.
They were lawyers and professors arguing in English in Calcutta drawing rooms.
Gandhi went to villages, wore what villagers wore, and organised farmers.
Then came *1919*. In Amritsar, a crowd of thousands gathered in a walled garden called *Jallianwala Bagh*.
A British brigadier marched troops to the entrance, blocked the only main exit,
and ordered them to fire into the crowd without warning. They fired for about ten minutes, until the ammunition was nearly gone.
The official death count was 379. Indian estimates ran well over a thousand.
The brigadier was relieved of command. He was also publicly celebrated by large parts of the British press and public,
and a fund was raised to give him a sizeable purse of money.
That did more for Indian independence than *any speech ever delivered*.
Gandhi's answer was to make British rule *impossible to operate* rather than impossible to defend.
The clearest example is *salt*.
Britain held a monopoly on salt. Indians were forbidden from collecting or making their own and had to buy taxed salt.
In a hot country, where everyone needs salt, and the poorest need it most.
So in March 1930, at sixty years old, *Gandhi walked*.
He set off from his ashram with *78 followers* and walked *385 kilometres* to the sea at *Dandi* over *24 days*,
and the crowd grew every day, and the world's newspapers followed the whole way.
On the morning of *6 April* he waded into the shallows and picked up a lump of natural salt from the mud.
That was the crime. Bending down and *picking up salt*.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Sir, he's picked up some salt.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Arrest him.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: We'd have to arrest quite a few people.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: How many?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Currently? The coastline.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Be specific.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Everyone is doing it, sir. Boiling seawater on their stoves. Grandmothers. Children.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Then arrest them.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: We arrested sixty thousand, sir. We're out of prisons.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: This is salt. It's mud. It's worth nothing.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Yes sir, that does appear to be the point.
Around *60,000* people were jailed. The salt tax survived a while longer, but the authority behind it didn't.
Then came the Second World War, which India was entered into without a single Indian being consulted.
Over *two million* Indians volunteered and fought, the largest volunteer army in history.
And in 1943, famine hit Bengal again. Around three million people died,
while wartime policy kept grain moving out of the province and refused offers of imported relief.
By *1945* Britain was victorious, exhausted and broke, and it was now obvious that it could not hold India.
So independence was coming. It came with a line on a map,
drawn by a man who had *never set foot in the country*.

title: Act 12: Five Weeks to Cut a Continent in Half

beats.text: His name was *Cyril Radcliffe*, he was a British lawyer, and he arrived in India in *July 1947*.
He had never been there before. That was considered *a qualification*, because it meant he had no local loyalties.
He was given roughly *five weeks* to draw the border that would divide British India into India and Pakistan,
splitting the provinces of *Punjab* and *Bengal* down the middle.
He worked from outdated maps and census data, in the heat, mostly in a bungalow,
deciding which villages would end up in which country.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: How long do I have?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: About five weeks.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: For what, exactly?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Punjab and Bengal. Where the line goes.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Have I been given accurate maps?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You've been given maps.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Population figures?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: From the last census.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Which was?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: That's six years ago. There's been a war.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Yes.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: And nobody local is advising me because—

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Because anyone local would have a preference, sir.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: And I don't?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You've never been here. That's rather the point.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Yes. I'm beginning to see the flaw in it.
The line was published on *17 August 1947*, two days after independence.
So for two days, tens of millions of people were free and had no idea which country they were in.
What followed was one of the largest and fastest movements of people in human history.
Somewhere between 10 and 15 million people crossed the new border in a few months.
Hindus and Sikhs moving one way, Muslims the other, often with what they could carry.
And it turned into slaughter. Trains arrived at stations with everyone aboard dead.
Estimates of the death toll run from several hundred thousand to two million.
Families that had lived in the same towns for centuries were on opposite sides overnight.
Gandhi spent independence day itself in Calcutta, fasting, trying to stop the killing there.
Five months later, on 30 January 1948, he was shot dead by a Hindu extremist who believed he had been too accommodating to Muslims.
Meanwhile at midnight on 14 August, *Jawaharlal Nehru* had stood up and told a free India
that at the stroke of the midnight hour, while the world slept, India would awake to life and freedom.
Both things were true on the same night. That's the thing about 1947.
It is the greatest day in modern Indian history and one of the worst, and there is no version where you get one without the other.

title: Act 13: 565 Kingdoms, Three Weeks of Money, and a Rocket to Mars

beats.text: Here's something most people outside India don't know.
In 1947, Britain only directly ruled about two-thirds of the place. The rest was *565* separate princely states,
technically independent, with their own rulers, and they all had to choose.
Bringing them in fell to *Vallabhbhai Patel*, and it is one of the most underrated administrative achievements of the century.
Most joined through negotiation. A few needed serious pressure.
*Hyderabad*, which was bigger than England and Scotland put together, was taken by military action in *1948*.
beats.fix: Script said Hyderabad was 'the size of France'. It was about 214,000 km² (France is about 550,000 km²); England plus Scotland is about 210,000 km².

beats.text: *Kashmir* chose India under invasion and is still contested today, which is why India and Pakistan have fought repeatedly over it ever since.
And then India did the thing nobody expected from a country that poor. *It held elections*.
Universal adult suffrage from the start, in 1951, for a population where more than 80 percent couldn't read,
beats.fix: Script said 'around 85 percent unable to read'. The 1951 census put literacy at about 18%, so just over 80% were unable to read.

beats.text: which meant ballot papers with *party symbols* instead of names.
It worked. *It's still how it's done*.
The next four decades were hard. India imported food to survive into the 1960s until the *Green Revolution* turned it into a grain exporter.
It fought China in 1962 and lost, fought Pakistan repeatedly, and in 1971 intervened in the war that created *Bangladesh*.
In 1975, Prime Minister *Indira Gandhi*, facing a court ruling against her election, declared a state of *Emergency*.
Opposition leaders jailed, press censored, elections suspended, for *21 months*.
And then, in 1977, for reasons historians still argue about, she called an election anyway.
She lost. Badly. And she *accepted it* and left office.
Then *1991*, and the moment that changed everything. India's foreign currency reserves fell to roughly *three weeks* of imports.
Three weeks from being unable to *buy oil*.
To get an emergency loan, India physically airlifted *47 tonnes* of its gold reserves to London as collateral,
and it had to be done quietly because the humiliation would have brought the government down.
Out of that came the reforms. Licence requirements scrapped, foreign investment allowed, currency devalued.
India stopped trying to make everything itself and opened up. Growth went from around *3 percent* a year to, in good years, *over 8*.
Then software. Indian engineers, cheap satellite bandwidth and a time zone exactly opposite America's built an IT industry out of almost nothing.
*Bangalore* went from a pensioners' town to a global tech centre in about fifteen years.
And in *2014*, India put a spacecraft into orbit around *Mars* on its first attempt, which no country had ever done.
It cost about *74 million dollars*, which is less than the Hollywood film *Gravity* cost to make.
A country that had been airlifting its gold to London 23 years earlier put a probe around another planet for less than a space movie.
So here's the thousand years.
A land so rich it was robbed seventeen times by the same man.
An empire founded by a homesick conqueror who complained about the melons.
A billion dollars of marble built for a grave.
A throne carried off to Persia.
A trading company that bought a province and taxed it through a famine.
A border drawn in five weeks by a man who'd never been there.
And a country that walked out of all of it, held elections it had no business being able to hold,
and is now the most populous nation on Earth and one of its largest economies.
The thing that strikes me, after all of it, is that nothing about India got erased.
Not by Ghazni, not by Aurangzeb, not by the Raj. The languages are still there. The temples are still there.
Hampi is still there, in ruins, with its stone chariot.
The country got taken apart repeatedly by people who assumed it was one thing they could conquer.
It was *never one thing*. That's precisely why it's still here.
And if you think a thousand years of India was chaotic, you should see what happened to the country next door
that was carved out of it on the same night. Click here for that one, and I'll catch you next time.
